full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I agree with the first pass, but for a different reason. The field rule isn't a minor twist on the voter model. It acts once, at the start, and erases one type. After that, the system is an ordinary 3-type voter model that starts with uneven proportions.

**Why the field rule is trivial (from your sub-program table)**
- **Rule 2 alone:** no spatial structure (Moran ≈ 0, correlation length 1, no reversals). Only 3 types survive, and type entropy is 0.753.
- **Normalised entropy for proportions (½, ¼, ¼) over 4 types:** 1.5 bits ÷ 2 bits = 0.75. That fits rule 2 turning almost every type-0 cell into type 2 near the start. Nothing in the program pushes field 0 back below 0.5 or reseeds type 0, so type 0 never comes back.
- **Full program:** entropy 0.743 and 3 types, which is just that skewed 3-type start plus the voter model's slow drift.
- **Rule 1 alone:** gives the same spatial statistics as the full program (Moran 0.517 vs 0.518, correlation length 3 vs 3, domains 6.1 vs 5.9). The two rules don't combine to produce anything new.
- **The "no sub-program matches" check:** this only fails because the voter model alone keeps 4 types and the field rule alone has no clustering. Each rule explains its own features. They don't interact, apart from the field rule shrinking the starting palette.

**What the behaviour actually is**
The clustering, correlation length, reversals and domain counts are textbook 2D voter-model coarsening. Dornic et al. show the two-dimensional voter model represents a broad class of models for which phase ordering takes place without surface tension. That paper is Phys. Rev. Lett. 87, 045701 (2001), arXiv:cond-mat/0101202. The voter model is described as having very irregular domain frontiers (which in physical terms stem from the absence of surface tension), and logarithmic coarsening. It also sits by construction right at a critical point, with diverging characteristic length and time scales. That fits the persistent cell flipping (g_reversals ≈ 0.76) and the many irregular domains that remain at 64×64. Redner's review attributes the missing surface tension to the update rule being linear in the number of disagreeing neighbours (no surface tension along an interface that separates domains).

**Genuine or artifact?**
- **Spatial features** (Moran, correlation length, domain count, reversals): genuine voter-model coarsening. They're real, but they come entirely from rule 1.
- **g_n_types and g_type_entropy:** artifacts of the field rule wiping out type 0 at the start. They are not emergent.
- **The "interaction" story:** misleading. The knock-out comparison credits these features to interaction, but the field coupling contributes nothing dynamically.

**Caveat:** I didn't open the Dornic et al. PDF itself, only its abstract and papers that cite it. The voter-model facts I rely on are standard and well established.
